title: ⭐ Practice: money, words and a first opinion

questions.prompt: Carol calls herself naïve about the business side of her career. Which words say the same thing?

options.text: already rich and famous
cruel and without pity
inexperienced and simple minded
well trained and very careful

questions.explanation: "inexperienced and simple minded" is the definition the book gives for naïve: she signs and trusts because she has not yet learnt how the trade works. "well trained and very careful" is the opposite. "already rich and famous" describes her situation, not her judgement, and "cruel and without pity" is the meaning of ruthless, the word she uses for show business itself.

questions.prompt: Carol says she feels closer to her mother than to anybody else. What does close mean in that sentence?

options.text: very near and intimate
living in the next street
quiet, calm and reserved
shut and locked for the night

questions.explanation: "very near and intimate" is the meaning of close here: the distance is one of feeling, not of metres, which is why the person you tell everything to is the closest one. "living in the next street" takes near in its physical sense only. "shut and locked for the night" is the verb to close, a different word with the same spelling, and "quiet, calm and reserved" describes a character, not a relationship.

questions.prompt: Carol answers one of the journalist's questions with an age: twenty-one. Only one question on his list can be answered like that. Which one?

options.text: At what age did you make your first album?
How old were you when you signed your first contract?
When did you sing in public for the first time?
When will you have access to your fortune?

questions.explanation: "When will you have access to your fortune?" is the one: the money is locked until Carol is twenty-one, and only a question about the future can be answered by an age she has not reached yet. The three other questions all ask about something that has already happened, so their answers would have to be ages below seventeen, the age she is now.

questions.prompt: Carol tells the journalist that other people's opinions do not matter to her. What is she saying?

options.text: She does not understand them.
She has never heard them.
They are not important to her.
They make her very angry indeed.

questions.explanation: "They are not important to her." is right: to matter means to be of importance, so something that does not matter carries no weight for you. "She does not understand them." would need a verb of understanding. "She has never heard them." says she does not know they exist, and "They make her very angry indeed." would mean the opposite, since a thing that angers you matters to you a great deal.

questions.prompt: Four pupils answer the questionnaire question about sharing pocket money. Which answer is the selfish one?

options.text: I keep every dinar for myself and never lend my brother any.
I lend some to my cousin whenever he has spent all of his own.
I put half of what I get aside to buy a present for my mother.
I share what I get with my little sister whenever she needs it.

questions.explanation: "I keep every dinar for myself and never lend my brother any." is the selfish answer: a selfish person thinks only of himself, and this one both keeps and refuses. The three others all send part of the money towards somebody else, by sharing, by buying a present or by lending, so none of them can be called selfish.

questions.prompt: Carol goes to a school where there are no boys. She tells the journalist that it is very good for her marks, but that it leaves her no chance to learn how to get on with boys. Which sentence reports her answer faithfully?

options.text: The school is bad for her marks but good for meeting boys.
The school is good for her marks but bad for meeting boys.
The school is good for her marks, so she will stay there next year.
The school is good for her marks and good for meeting boys.

questions.explanation: "The school is good for her marks but bad for meeting boys." reports her faithfully: she says one good thing and one bad thing about the same school, and a faithful report keeps both halves and keeps each one on its own side. "The school is bad for her marks but good for meeting boys." keeps two halves but swaps them over. "The school is good for her marks and good for meeting boys." drops the price she pays and leaves only the advantage. "The school is good for her marks, so she will stay there next year." adds a decision that she never makes.
